title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Russian has two futures, and which one you get is decided by the VERB, not by what you mean. A verb of the everyday kind — the M4 kind — builds its future with búdu plus the dictionary form: Závtra ya búdu rabótat'. A verb of the finished-event kind — the M5 kind — has no búdu future at all: its present-tense shape IS its future. Závtra ya kuplyú khleb is "tomorrow I will buy bread", with a form that looks like a present tense.

So búdu is not "will". It is half of one of the two futures, and it never touches the other half: Ya búdu kupít' and Ya búdu poytí do not exist, in the way that "I will to buy" does not exist in English. If the verb is one of M5's finished-event pair, drop búdu and use the verb alone.

búdu · búdete · búdet is the same word as M5's byl. Russian's "be" has a real past, a real future, and nothing at all in the present — that is the whole of it, and "Russian has no verb to be" was only ever true of the middle one.
Negation has not moved since M3: ne goes in front of the finite verb, which in a búdu future means in front of búdu and never in front of the dictionary form. Závtra ya ne búdu rabótat'.

The present tense can also be a future when a time word makes it obvious — Závtra ya rabótayu is ordinary Russian for a fixed arrangement, exactly as English says "I'm working tomorrow". It is not taught as a pattern here, but it is worth recognising.

words.note: Tomorrow. It opens the sentence, the way vcherá did, and it anchors every line on this rung. Never changes shape.

sentences.trap: búdu carries the future and rabótat' stays in its dictionary shape — the same shape it had after khochú in M3. Only one verb in a Russian sentence ever takes an ending.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ya BOO-doo ra-BO-tat'. The v of závtra is said as an f, as it is in vcherá and vsegdá.

variations.changed: swap the second verb — any of M3's or M4's dictionary shapes drops into the slot
ne in front of búdu, never in front of rabótat'
búdu → búdete for the polite you, and the question adds nothing

mistake.why: Two verbs cannot both carry an ending. búdu takes it; rabótat' stays in its dictionary shape.

sentences.usage: Plans for tomorrow — the pattern you can build yourself out of anything M3 and M4 taught.
sentences.mnemonic: One ending per sentence. búdu takes it, the other verb waits in its dictionary clothes.

words.cue: to rest · to relax · to be on holiday
words.note: One word for resting, relaxing and being on holiday — Russians otdykháyut at the seaside for a fortnight and also for ten minutes on a bench. Pattern I: otdykháyu (I), otdykháyete (you, polite).

sentences.trap: English picks a different word for each size of rest — rest, relax, be on holiday. Russian uses this one for all three, so the sentence is vaguer than its English translations and that is not a problem.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ya BOO-doo ad-dy-KHAT'. Two unstressed o letters at the front of otdykhát', both flattened; the kh near the end is the raspy one.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will rest at home
variations.changed: M5's dóma on the end — no preposition needed
the polite you-form of búdu, and the time word moved to the end
ne in front of búdu, and závtra dropped altogether

mistake.why: A dictionary shape cannot stand alone as the sentence's verb. It needs búdu in front of it, or an ending of its own.

sentences.usage: Weekends, holidays, and the answer to "what are you doing tomorrow?".
sentences.mnemonic: One Russian word covers every size of rest, from a bench to a fortnight.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I will write a letter

words.note: "I will write" — and there is no búdu anywhere. This is a finished-event verb, like M5's kupít', so its present-looking shape is its future: napishú (I), napíshete (you, polite). Its past is napisál · napisála. The na- on the front is what makes it the finished kind.

sentences.trap: Nothing in napishú looks like a future, and that is exactly the difficulty. The ending is the ordinary I-ending; the tense comes from which verb of the pair you chose, and this one has no present tense at all.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ya na-pee-SHOO pees'-MO. The sh of napishú is a hard sh, made with the tongue pulled back — harder than the English one.

variations.changed: the same verb in the past — the shape a man writes; a woman writes napisála

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will write the newspaper
variations.changed: swap the object — and it bends, being feminine: gazétu
the polite you-form — still no búdu in the sentence

mistake.why: búdu belongs only with the everyday kind of verb. napishú is already the future all by itself.

sentences.usage: Promising to do one particular thing — the future Russians use most.
sentences.mnemonic: A finished-event verb has no present tense, so its present-shaped form is free to be the future.

words.cue: I will call · I will phone
words.note: "I will call", on the telephone. Another finished-event verb, so again no búdu: pozvonyú (I), pozvoníte (you, polite). Its past is pozvoníl · pozvoníla. It shares a root with M1's Menyá zovút — both are about calling, one on the phone and one by name.

sentences.trap: English needs something after "call" — call you, call back, give you a call. Russian is happy with the verb on its own, and adding a word for "you" here would need a shape this level has not taught.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ya pa-zva-NYOO. Three syllables before the stress, all light, then the weight lands right at the end.

variations.changed: the time word at the end instead of the front — both orders are ordinary
the same verb in the past, from a man — pozvoníla from a woman
the polite you-form, and still no búdu anywhere

mistake.why: The same cross-wiring as S03. pozvonyú is the whole future; búdu has no business in front of it.

sentences.usage: Arranging to be in touch — one of the most useful promises in the language.
sentences.mnemonic: If the verb is one of M5's finished-event kind, it does the future on its own.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I will buy a present

words.note: A present. Masculine, and a thing rather than a creature, so it does not change as the object.

sentences.trap: kuplyú is M5's kupíl, one row and one word — the past and the future of the same verb, with no present tense in between. Tapping either shape opens the same note, and that is deliberate.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ya koo-PLYOO pa-DA-rak. kuplyú grows an l the way lyublyú does, and the stress moves onto it.

variations.changed: the same verb in the past — one word, two tenses, no present

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will buy a ticket
variations.changed: swap the thing bought — neither word around it moves

variations.cue: I want to buy a present
variations.changed: M3's frame — after khochú the verb goes back to its dictionary shape, kupít'

mistake.why: kuplyú is already the future. búdu goes only with the everyday kind of verb, and this is not one.

sentences.usage: Shopping plans, birthdays, and anything you intend to get done once.
sentences.mnemonic: One row, two tenses, and the empty space between them is the present.

words.note: An exam. Masculine, and borrowed — the z in the middle is a plain z and the whole word is close enough to English to be free.

sentences.trap: Two words, and both of them are nouns — no verb at all. The zero copula from M1 is still running, and a time word plus a noun is a complete Russian sentence about the future.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ek-ZA-myen. The eh at the front is a plain open "e", the letter Russian keeps for exactly this job.

variations.cue: Tomorrow there will be an exam
variations.changed: búdet spelled out — the same fact, with the future said rather than left to the time word
the past cannot be left out: byl is obligatory where búdet was optional

variations.cue: Tomorrow there is an exam in the morning
variations.changed: M4's time word on the end, and still no verb in the sentence

mistake.why: yest' is not a present tense of "to be" — M1's rule holds. Závtra ehkzámen, or Závtra búdet ehkzámen.

sentences.usage: Announcing what is happening — the shortest complete sentence about the future you can write.
sentences.mnemonic: In the present the verb is missing; in the future it is optional; in the past it is obligatory.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I will read a lot

words.note: "A lot", covering English's much and many at once. It goes in front of the verb, in the same seat as M4's chásto and vsegdá. In front of a noun it changes that noun's ending — a job this level does not teach — so here it only ever describes a verb.

sentences.trap: English splits much and many by whether you can count the thing. Russian does not split them at all, and mnógo covers both.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ya BOO-doo MNO-ga chee-TAT'. The m and n at the start of mnógo run together, and the final o flattens to "a".

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will work a lot
variations.changed: swap the second verb — mnógo keeps its place in front of it
back to M4's present — mnógo sits in exactly the same seat there

variations.display: Závtra ya ne búdu mnógo chitát'.
variations.script: Завтра я не буду много читать.
variations.cue: Tomorrow I will not read a lot
variations.changed: ne in front of búdu, and mnógo stays where it was

mistake.why: Understandable, and it throws an odd emphasis onto mnógo. It belongs in front of the verb it describes.

sentences.usage: Saying how much of something you will do — and mnógo is the same word for countable and uncountable alike.
sentences.mnemonic: much and many are one word here, and it goes where chásto goes.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I will get up late

words.note: "I will get up" — the finished-event partner of M4's vstayú, and a different word from it, not a different tense. vstayú is what you do every morning; vstánu is what you will do once, tomorrow. Its past is vstal · vstála.
Late — the opposite of M4's ráno, and it sits in the same place, after the verb. The d in the middle is not said: "POZ-na".

sentences.trap: M4's vstayú and this vstánu differ by two letters and by everything else. One is a habit and has a present tense; the other is a single event and has none, which is why it can be a future.
sentences.sound: ZAV-tra ya FSTA-noo POZ-na. The d of pózdno is dropped entirely, the way the t of chásto nearly is.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will get up early
variations.changed: swap the time word — M4's ráno, in the same seat
M4's habit verb — every day, not tomorrow
the same finished-event verb in the past, from a man

mistake.why: vstánu is already the future. búdu belongs with vstavát', the habit verb — and even then it would say something else.

sentences.usage: Weekend plans — and the clearest side-by-side of the two halves of a verb pair.
sentences.mnemonic: Two verbs, two lives: one has a present and no future of its own, the other has a future and no present.

words.note: "You will come" — a finished-event verb, so no búdu. pridyóte (you, polite), pridú (I), pridyót (he or she). The yó is written, as always in this course, and as always it carries the stress.

sentences.trap: It looks like a present tense and asks about tomorrow. By now that should be expected: with this half of a verb pair, the present-shaped ending is the only future there is.
sentences.sound: vy pree-DYO-tye ZAV-tra. The yó is stressed, as every yó is, so the middle of the word is where the weight lands.

variations.changed: the answer, in the I-form — pridú, and the yó disappears when the stress moves
the he/she form, yó still in place

variations.cue: Will you come in the evening?
variations.changed: M4's time word instead of závtra — the question frame is unchanged

mistake.why: pridyóte is the whole future already. Two future markers in one sentence is one too many.

sentences.usage: Inviting somebody, or checking that they are coming — the most useful question on this rung.
sentences.mnemonic: yó is always stressed. When the stress leaves, so does the yó: pridyóte, but pridú.

words.note: "Of course." Written with a ch and said with a sh — ka-NYESH-na — which is one of the few Russian words whose spelling and sound genuinely disagree. It is set off by a comma at the front of the sentence.

sentences.trap: The spelling lies. Almost every Russian word is said as it is written; this one, and a handful like it, are not, and no rule will help you — it has to be remembered.
sentences.sound: ka-NYESH-na ya BOO-doo ra-BO-tat'. The chn of konéchno is said "shn", not "chn".

variations.changed: swap the promise — Konéchno takes any statement after its comma
on its own, as a whole answer

variations.cue: Of course I will not work
variations.changed: ne in front of búdu, with Konéchno untouched at the front

mistake.why: The comma is not optional in Russian: Konéchno is set off from the sentence it introduces, always.

sentences.usage: Agreeing warmly — and it is one of the first words you will hear in reply to a request.
sentences.mnemonic: Written with ch, said with sh. There is no rule; there is only this word.

comprehensionPool.cue: Tomorrow I will buy a ticket
Anna will come in the evening
Tomorrow I will get up early
Tomorrow I will go home early
Will you buy a present tomorrow?
